title: The Chair the Parliament Made: Lie, the Arrest at Fontainebleau, and the Groups That Move
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Nordfjordeid, birth at the parsonage
stops.date_confidence: attested: MacTutor, Store norske leksikon and Wikipedia all give 17 December 1842 at Nordfjordeid. The pin is the village centre; no parsonage building footprint was confirmed. A baptismal record of 3 May 1843 and a vaccination record of 14 August 1843 are cited by the dossier from the Historical Population Register and were not independently checked.
stops.campa: In the parsonage at Nordfjordeid, where the fjord narrows under the mountains of Nordfjord, Marius Sophus Lie is born on the seventeenth of December, the youngest of six children of the parish priest Johan Herman Lie and his wife Mette Maren Stabell. The house is a Lutheran vicarage of the ordinary Norwegian kind: sermons, a glebe, a congregation strung out along the water. Norway is joined to Sweden under one crown, and its only university, at Christiania, is twenty-nine years old. The parish has one priest in it and it is his father.
suggested_refs: The Eid parsonage at Nordfjordeid, where Johan Herman Lie served; the later monument to Lie in the village
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Moss, the family crosses the country
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed year: Store norske leksikon says the father served at Moss from 1851; no month or day is recorded. The pin is the town centre, not a confirmed residence.
stops.campa: The father takes a new clerical post and the family crosses the country, from the western fjords to the port of Moss on the eastern side of the Oslofjord. The boy is eight. Moss is timber and shipping and a paper mill, a working town on a working strait, and here Sophus first goes to school. Which school, the sources do not say. The name Moss borgerlige Realskole attaches to him only in later retellings; MacTutor records nothing beyond the town, which it calls a port in south-eastern Norway and leaves at that.
suggested_refs: Parish records of Moss for the incumbency of Johan Herman Lie from 1851
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Moss, the death of Mette Maren Stabell
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Store norske leksikon places the mother's death when Lie was about nine, i.e. 1852. No exact date was found in any source consulted, and her birth and death years are absent from snl.no, both Wikipedias and MacTutor.
stops.campa: Mette Maren Stabell dies about a year after the family settles in Moss. Sophus is nine. Her people were from Trondheim, a well-known family there, and past that the record on her is almost blank: no birth year that any reference source will state, no death date, nothing about what she was to the youngest of her children. The father continues the household alone and will outlive her by more than twenty years. Whether the boy was in the house when she died, no register anyone has consulted says.
suggested_refs: Norwegian burial registers for Moss, 1852, for the death of Mette Maren Stabell

segments.name: Christiania: the School, the University, and the Years Without a Subject

stops.name: Nissen's Latin- og Realskole, the boy sent to the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested year: MacTutor and Store norske leksikon both give 1857 for the entry at Nissen's; month and day unknown. The pin is Rosenkrantz' gate 7, the school's building from 1847 per Norwegian Wikipedia, about seventy metres from the coordinates carried by the research pool.
stops.campa: At fifteen he is sent to Christiania and enrolled at Nissen's Latin- og Realskole in Rosenkrantz' gate, a private school founded in 1843 whose pupils are the sons of the capital's professional class. Mathematics does not single him out. What the school gives him instead is Ernst Motzfeldt, a fellow pupil who becomes the friend of his life and the recipient of his most unguarded letters, and a building he will come back to as a paid tutor when the university cannot keep him fed. He boards in the capital on his father's money, and the money is a country priest's.
suggested_refs: Nissens latin- og realskole, Rosenkrantz' gate 7, Christiania, the Nebelong building of 1847
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Royal Frederick University, the examen artium
stops.date_confidence: attested year, month and day unknown: Store norske leksikon and MacTutor give 1859 for the examen artium and matriculation. The pin is Domus Academica, Karl Johans gate 47, in use from 1851, corrected from the pool's coordinates by about 185 metres.
stops.campa: He passes the examen artium with strong marks and enters the Royal Frederick University, in the Domus Academica on Karl Johans gate, a building eight years old. Norway's only university is small enough that a student can know every professor by sight. Lie reads mathematics and the natural sciences and distinguishes himself in neither, and no teacher there marks him out for anything. He sits the qualifying examination only in 1865, six years after matriculating.
suggested_refs: Domus Academica, Karl Johans gate 47, main building of the Royal Frederick University from 1851
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Royal Frederick University, Sylow lectures on Abel and Galois
stops.date_confidence: attested year: MacTutor states verbatim that Lie attended lectures by Ludvig Sylow in 1862. Month and day are not recorded. An earlier pass of this research wrongly marked the claim unverifiable; the source says it plainly.
stops.campa: Ludvig Sylow, a schoolmaster standing in at the university, lectures on the theory of equations and expounds Abel and Galois to whoever will come. Lie comes. Evariste Galois has been thirty years dead, shot in a Paris duel at twenty, and his notion that a group of symmetries governs whether an equation can be solved is still being unpacked by the men whose books Sylow is reading from. Nothing happens at once. The word group enters Lie's vocabulary in that room, from a schoolmaster standing in, ten years before he begins building a theory of groups that vary continuously.
suggested_refs: Ludvig Sylow's 1862 Christiania lectures on the theory of equations, after Abel and Galois
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Christiania, the years he later called wasted
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the qualifying examination (MacTutor); the surrounding characterisation of 1864-68 comes from Lie's own letter to Ernst Motzfeldt as quoted by MacTutor, which gives no precise date or archive reference for the letter.
stops.campa: He takes his qualifying examination and then does very little with it. He tutors at his old school, he reads, he applies for a travel scholarship and does not get it. For three years the record shows a man in his twenties in a small northern capital with no position, no subject, and no reason for anyone to expect anything of him at all. He is not idle so much as unassigned. Writing to Motzfeldt long afterwards, he set the period down without softening it.
stops.quote: ...in the years 1864-68, I really underestimated my own mental power.
stops.quote_source: Lie to Ernst Motzfeldt, undated, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'
suggested_refs: The Lie-Motzfeldt correspondence, source of most of what is known about Lie's private judgement of himself
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Christiania, waking Motzfeldt in the middle of the night
stops.date_confidence: traditional, year attested: MacTutor dates Lie's first original mathematical idea to 1867 and gives the anecdote in these words. It is an oral tradition rendered in English by MacTutor, not a documentary transcript, and MacTutor does not say which discovery it was. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: In the middle of a night in 1867 an idea arrives. He does not wait for morning and does not write it down and sleep on it. He crosses Christiania to Ernst Motzfeldt's lodgings, wakes his friend out of bed, and shouts it at him. Which idea it was the anecdote does not preserve, only that it was the first of his own and that others followed. He is twenty-four, has published nothing, holds no post, and has spent three years telling himself he may not be good for much. Motzfeldt, sitting up in the dark, hears it out.
stops.quote: I have found it, it is quite simple!
stops.quote_source: Lie to Ernst Motzfeldt, 1867, as given in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'
suggested_refs: MacTutor's account of Lie's first original idea, 1867, and the Motzfeldt anecdote attached to it
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Christiania, the pamphlet he paid to print
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and for the self-financed printing: MacTutor states that Lie wrote a short paper in 1869 which he published at his own expense, and that a travel scholarship followed. The figure of roughly 245 lifetime publications, sometimes attached to this stop, is not in MacTutor, Wikipedia or snl.no and is carried here as reconstruction only.
stops.campa: He writes a short paper on the representation of imaginary elements in plane geometry and, no one being willing to print it for him, pays for the printing himself. Part appears in Christiania at his own expense; part reaches Crelle's Journal in Berlin, which is where a Norwegian goes to be read at all. The pamphlet is an argument for a travel scholarship as much as a piece of mathematics, and it works. The university gives him money to go to Germany. He is twenty-six and has never left Norway.
suggested_refs: Lie's 1869 paper on the representation of imaginary elements in plane geometry, privately printed at Christiania and in part in Crelle's Journal
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Gottingen, the first Continental university
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stop, month approximate: MacTutor records the Gottingen visit on the way south in late 1869. The pin is the canonical Gottingen university coordinate already carried elsewhere in the corpus.
stops.campa: On the way south he stops at Gottingen. It is his first sight of a Continental university at work: a mathematical faculty with a library, a seminar and a tradition, all three of which Christiania lacks. He stays briefly. What Gottingen is for, in the autumn of 1869, is the road to Berlin, and he is on that road with a scholarship in his pocket and no reputation to go in front of him. MacTutor records the stop and nothing about what he did there. The visit is a line in an itinerary.
suggested_refs: The Georg-August-Universitat and its mathematical library, visited on the 1869 journey south
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Berlin, meeting Felix Klein
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia dates the Berlin stay September 1869 to February 1870 and names Kronecker, Weierstrass and Kummer; MacTutor corroborates the visit and the meeting with Klein. Exact day unknown, defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: Berlin in the winter of 1869 is Kummer, Weierstrass and Kronecker, the most rigorous mathematics being done anywhere, and Lie finds it uncongenial. He goes to the seminar. He is not converted to the analytic style, and the analytic style takes no particular notice of him. What Berlin gives him is Felix Klein, twenty years old, geometric in temperament exactly where Lie is geometric, and quick in the way Lie is slow. They recognise each other within days. For the next three years they will work in each other's pockets.
suggested_refs: The University of Berlin seminar under Kummer and Weierstrass, winter 1869-70
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Paris, the spring with Klein
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay and the contacts (English Wikipedia and MacTutor); the month is approximate, both sources giving only spring 1870. The pin is the canonical Paris centroid used across the corpus rather than a meeting address, none of which is recorded.
stops.campa: In the spring the two of them move to Paris and lodge together. Gaston Darboux receives them. So does Camille Jordan, whose treatise on substitutions has just turned Galois's groups into a working instrument, and so does Michel Chasles. What the two of them arrive at that spring is that groups are not a curiosity of algebra but the way a geometry is organised. Klein will publish it in 1872 as the Erlangen Program; Lie will spend his life developing the continuous case. Klein is twenty-one and Lie is twenty-seven.
suggested_refs: Camille Jordan, Traite des substitutions et des equations algebriques (1870), read by Lie in Paris that spring
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Paris, the declaration of war and the road south
stops.date_confidence: attested: France declared war on Prussia on 19 July 1870, and English Wikipedia records that Klein, a Prussian subject, left Paris while Lie, a neutral Norwegian, remained and then set out on foot toward Italy. The day of Lie's own departure is not recorded.
stops.campa: France declares war on Prussia on the nineteenth of July. Klein is a Prussian subject in an enemy capital and leaves at once. Lie is Norwegian, a neutral, and stays on; then, restless and short of money, he decides to walk to Italy. He puts his papers in a knapsack and goes south on foot through a country mobilising for invasion: a tall fair-haired foreigner in walking clothes, carrying letters written in German and sheets of mathematics that nobody along the road can read.
suggested_refs: The French declaration of war of 19 July 1870 and the emptying of Paris of Prussian subjects
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Fontainebleau, arrested as a German spy
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the arrest, the espionage suspicion, the month of roughly August 1870, the imprisonment of about a month and Darboux's intervention (MacTutor and English Wikipedia). No exact arrest date, no interrogation record, no police dossier number and no named place of detention were located by any source consulted. The pin is the canonical Fontainebleau coordinate already carried in the corpus.
stops.campa: Some sixty kilometres out of Paris he is stopped at Fontainebleau and arrested as a German spy. MacTutor puts it flatly: his mathematics notes were assumed to be top secret coded messages, and the German correspondence in his pack read as orders. He is held about a month. Gaston Darboux comes down from Paris and vouches for him, the suspicion is not sustained, and he is let go. No interrogation record survives, no arrest date, no name for the room he was kept in. The whole episode is known only from what he and his friends said afterwards.
suggested_refs: The chateau town of Fontainebleau, where Lie was held for roughly four weeks in the summer of 1870
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Dusseldorf, the collaboration resumed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, weakest-attested stretch of the life: the route out of France through Switzerland and Italy and the November reunion with Klein at Dusseldorf rest on the German biographical literature cited by the dossier (Fritzsche). MacTutor was fetched and searched: the words Switzerland and Dusseldorf do not appear in it, and it supplies no post-release itinerary at all.
stops.campa: Out of prison and out of France, he goes south and east through Switzerland into Italy, then turns north again into Germany. At Dusseldorf he finds Klein, and the interrupted work resumes for a few weeks in the country that has just beaten the one he was arrested in. This is the thinnest-documented passage of his life. The German biographies carry the route from Fontainebleau to the Rhine; the English reference articles do not mention it at all, supplying no itinerary between the prison and the return home, and no source anywhere names a date for the meeting.
suggested_refs: Fritzsche's reconstruction of Lie's autumn 1870 itinerary, the sole authority for the Dusseldorf stop
sources: Dossier's citation of Fritzsche's biographical studies of Lie, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Christiania, home with a subject
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month reconstructed: MacTutor and English Wikipedia confirm the 1870 return to Christiania, but neither specifies December in the text fetched. The month is carried from the dossier.
stops.campa: He comes home to Christiania after a year abroad, with no position waiting and a head full of Germany and France. Norway has one university, one chair of mathematics, and no obvious place for a twenty-eight-year-old whose foreign record includes a scholarship and an arrest. What he brings back instead is a question, and every paper he publishes for the next twenty-eight years will be some part of it: what happens to a geometry when you let its transformations vary continuously.
suggested_refs: Lie's Christiania notebooks of 1870-71, the first working out of continuous transformation groups
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Royal Frederick University, the dissertation
stops.date_confidence: the dissertation is dated 1871 (English Wikipedia). The award of the degree is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is left open: Store norske leksikon compresses it to a 1871 doctorate, MacTutor and English Wikipedia both give July 1872. Month and day of the dissertation are unknown.
stops.campa: He takes a scholarship and an assistantship at the university, teaches at Nissen's again to make the rent, and produces 'Over en Classe geometriske Transformationer,' on a class of geometric transformations. The title page is dated 1871. When the degree was actually conferred, the sources refuse to agree: the Norwegian national encyclopedia compresses it to 1871, the standard English accounts give July 1872, and nobody has reconciled the two. He is twenty-eight.
suggested_refs: Sophus Lie, Over en Classe geometriske Transformationer (Christiania, 1871)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Erlangen, the year of the Program
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the second 1872 German journey, taking in Gottingen and Erlangen with Klein, is carried by the German biographical literature (Fritzsche, Rowe) as cited in the dossier and is absent from MacTutor and both Wikipedias. The Erlangen Program itself is securely dated to 1872. Month is a placeholder for ordering.
stops.campa: Klein is called to a chair at Erlangen, and Lie travels to Germany again to see him, by way of Gottingen. The Erlangen Program is written this year: a geometry is the study of what a group of transformations leaves unchanged. Behind it sits Arthur Cayley's projective definition of distance of 1859, which Klein had read as a working model of non-Euclidean space. What passes between the two men in these weeks is what they will fight about twenty years later. No letter or note from that autumn survives to say what it was.
suggested_refs: Felix Klein, Vergleichende Betrachtungen uber neuere geometrische Forschungen (Erlangen, 1872), the Erlangen Program
sources: Dossier's citation of Fritzsche and Rowe on the 1872 journey, not independently confirmed
arthur_cayley.journey.json, for Klein's 1871 reading of Cayley's 1859 memoir on quantics

stops.name: Christiania, a chair invented by act of parliament
stops.date_confidence: the 1872 extraordinary personal professorship is attested (English Wikipedia, MacTutor, Store norske leksikon). The day-dates that circulate for it, 26 March for the parliamentary act and 1 July for the appointment, appear in none of MacTutor, en/no/de.wikipedia or snl.no and are reconstruction from the dossier's citation of Fritzsche. The date field is therefore the year alone.
stops.campa: The Storting votes an extraordinary personal professorship for Lie: not a vacancy filled but a chair invented, by act of parliament, for one twenty-nine-year-old. Norway has decided it will not lose this one the way it lost Niels Henrik Abel, dead at twenty-six of tuberculosis and poverty while the great academies of Europe were still making up their minds about him. The salary is public money, voted by legislators who could not read a line of the work. He has security for the first time in his life.
suggested_refs: The Storting's 1872 act creating an extraordinary personal professorship for Lie; the second such act of 1894
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Risor, marriage to Anna Sophie Birch
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and town by Store norske leksikon, which gives 11 August 1874 at Risor; the year is corroborated by English Wikipedia. The church as venue is an assumption and was not confirmed. The pin is Risor kirke, built 1647.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of August, at Risor on the Skagerrak coast, Sophus Lie marries Anna Sophie Birch. He is thirty-one. They have been engaged since the end of 1872, when she was eighteen, or twenty; the sources give her birth as 1854 and as 1852 and are not reconciled. Three children will come: Marie Sofie, Anna Dagny, and Herman. Sixteen years from now she is the one who will travel into Germany, fetch her husband out of an asylum, and bring him back to Leipzig.
suggested_refs: Risor kirke, the town's church of 1647, presumed venue of the marriage of 11 August 1874

stops.name: Christiania, Ueber Gruppen von Transformationen
stops.date_confidence: attested year (MacTutor), which calls it a landmark early publication of the theory of continuous transformation groups. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: He publishes 'Ueber Gruppen von Transformationen,' and with it the programme of the rest of his life. The objects are groups whose elements vary continuously, the transformations of a space that slide into one another by degrees instead of being counted off. Nobody has asked him for this. He has no seminar around him and no student who can follow the argument to its end. He writes in German, because the few men anywhere who might one day check the work are in Germany, and there are none at all in Norway.
suggested_refs: Sophus Lie, 'Ueber Gruppen von Transformationen' (1874)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

segments.name: Abel, the Archiv, and the Arrival of Engel

stops.name: Christiania, editing Abel with Sylow
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline (English Wikipedia): a state-supported new edition of Abel's complete works by Lie and Sylow, published in two volumes in 1881 by Grondahl and Son. The start year is contradicted: English Wikipedia elsewhere dates the beginning of the collaboration to 1872 rather than 1873. The 1881 imprint was not independently re-fetched as a bibliographic record.
stops.campa: The state votes money for a new edition of the complete works of Niels Henrik Abel, and Lie and Ludvig Sylow are appointed to make it. The work takes eight years and comes out in two volumes from Grondahl and Son in 1881. Sylow had handed him Galois from a lectern in 1862; now the state hands the two of them Abel, and getting a dead genius properly into print is a national duty with a budget line. Lie says plainly and often that Sylow did the larger share of the work.
suggested_refs: Oeuvres completes de Niels Henrik Abel, ed. Sylow and Lie, 2 vols. (Christiania: Grondahl and Son, 1881)

stops.name: Christiania, founding the Archiv
stops.date_confidence: attested year (English Wikipedia) for the founding with Jacob Worm-Muller and Georg Ossian Sars. The characterisation of the journal as partly a reaction against conservative forces in Norwegian science comes from Store norske leksikon by way of the dossier and was not independently re-fetched.
stops.campa: With the physician Jacob Worm-Muller and the zoologist Georg Ossian Sars, Lie founds a journal, Archiv for Mathematik og Naturvidenskab, so that Norwegian science has somewhere of its own to put its work. Until now a Norwegian result went abroad to be printed, to Crelle's Journal in Berlin or somewhere like it, or else it was not printed at all. The Norwegian encyclopedia describes the founding partly as a move against the conservative forces then holding the country's scientific establishment.
suggested_refs: Archiv for Mathematik og Naturvidenskab, founded at Christiania in 1876

stops.name: Christiania, three children and no readers
stops.date_confidence: birth years attested for Marie Sofie (1877), Anna Dagny (1880) and Herman (1884) via English Wikipedia. The exact day of 22 April 1884 for Herman appears in no source consulted and is reconstruction. The stop is dated to the first birth to order the segment.
stops.campa: Marie Sofie is born in 1877, Anna Dagny in 1880, and in 1884 a son, Johan Herman, called Herman, after his grandfather the priest at Nordfjordeid. The household is a professor's household in a capital of a hundred thousand, and the professor works alone. Through these years Lie publishes steadily and is read by almost nobody: the papers are in German, the ideas are unfamiliar, and the handful of men in Europe equipped to judge them are busy with other things.
suggested_refs: Norwegian parish registers for the births of Marie Sofie, Anna Dagny and Johan Herman Lie

stops.name: Christiania, Friedrich Engel comes north
stops.date_confidence: attested year: MacTutor says Engel went to work with Lie in Christiania starting in 1884 and left in 1885; English Wikipedia gives 1884 for the arrival. The month of September, carried by the dossier, is in neither source and is reconstruction.
stops.campa: Friedrich Engel, twenty-three, arrives from Leipzig on a travelling scholarship to find out what Lie is actually doing. He stays into the following year, through a Christiania winter. Lie talks and Engel writes, and out of that division of labour comes the plan for a systematic treatise: Lie supplying the geometric sight and the flood of results, Engel supplying the analytic patience to put them in order and the willingness to be second on the title page.
suggested_refs: The Lie-Engel collaboration of 1884-85 at Christiania, origin of Theorie der Transformationsgruppen
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Drammensveien 84, the last Norwegian year
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the address comes from the dossier's citation of the Historical Population Register (histreg.no), which was not independently re-fetched. The pin is an approximate modern location on Drammensveien; the 1885 building and lot were not confirmed.
stops.campa: The population register puts the family at Drammensveien 84, on the western road out of the city, in the last full year before Germany. Lie is a professor with a chair made for him by parliament, a wife, three children and a correspondence that now runs south every week. Engel has gone back to Saxony carrying the notes for a treatise neither of them has written yet. Klein is about to move to Gottingen, and the best mathematical chair in Saxony will stand empty behind him.
suggested_refs: Historical Population Register (histreg.no) entry placing Lie at Drammensveien 84 in 1885
sources: Dossier's citation of the Historical Population Register, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Seeburgstrasse, the family arrives in Leipzig
stops.date_confidence: the 1886 Leipzig appointment as Klein's successor is attested (MacTutor, English Wikipedia). The Seeburgstrasse address and the February arrival come from the dossier's citation of Fritzsche and were not independently confirmed; the pin is an approximate placement on the historic street with no house number.
stops.campa: The family arrives in Leipzig and takes an apartment on Seeburgstrasse. Lie has accepted the chair Klein has vacated for Gottingen: a real German professorship, with students, an institute, and a mathematical public that can read him. He is forty-three. He leaves the country that invented a chair to keep him, for the country where his work is understood, and Norway lets him go. The street, the month and the house number all rest on a single German biography.
suggested_refs: Fritzsche's account of the Lie household's first Leipzig address on Seeburgstrasse
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'
Dossier's citation of Fritzsche for the address

stops.name: Augustusplatz, the inaugural lecture
stops.date_confidence: the lecture and its title are attested by German Wikipedia, which independently confirms 'Uber den Einfluss der Geometrie auf die Entwicklung der Mathematik' for 1886. The exact day of 29 May and the attendance of King Albert of Saxony are reconstruction: no source consulted gives the day, and German Wikipedia explicitly records no royal attendance. Month kept as May for ordering only.
stops.campa: In the Augusteum on Augustusplatz he gives his inaugural lecture, 'Uber den Einfluss der Geometrie auf die Entwicklung der Mathematik,' on the influence of geometry upon the development of mathematics. It is a manifesto as much as a formality: the geometric way of seeing, set against the analytic rigour of Berlin, by a man who was bored by Weierstrass at twenty-six and has not changed his mind since. The tradition that the King of Saxony sat in the hall is contradicted by the German account, which records no royal presence at all.
suggested_refs: The Augusteum on Augustusplatz, Leipzig, demolished 1968; Lie's inaugural lecture of 1886
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Bruderstrasse, the Spectatorium and the students
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the identification of Czermak's Spectatorium on Bruderstrasse as Lie's lecture hall, and the student roll attached to it, come from the dossier's citation and were not confirmed by any source fetched. The pin is a rough placement on the historic street. The date orders the segment and carries no evidential weight.
stops.campa: He lectures, by the German tradition, in Czermak's Spectatorium on Bruderstrasse, a hall built for physiological demonstrations. Through it pass Friedrich Engel, Georg Scheffers, Eduard Study, Felix Hausdorff, Gerhard Kowalewski and the Pole Kazimierz Zorawski. His way is to think aloud at the board, geometrically, and the students who can follow him remember it for the rest of their lives. Hausdorff will go on to found a topology Lie never saw. The lecture hall itself rests on one source and no other account names it.
suggested_refs: Czermak's Spectatorium, Bruderstrasse 32, Leipzig, named by the German biographical tradition as Lie's lecture hall
sources: Dossier's citation naming the Spectatorium and the Leipzig student cohort, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Leipzig, the first volume of the Theorie
stops.date_confidence: attested year and publisher: MacTutor gives Volume I of Theorie der Transformationsgruppen, on the general foundations of continuous transformation groups, from B. G. Teubner at Leipzig in 1888. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Volume I of Theorie der Transformationsgruppen appears from B. G. Teubner: the general foundations of continuous transformation groups, the whole apparatus set out in order for the first time. Engel is named on it as collaborator, and what that means in practice is that Engel wrote most of the prose. A theory that had lived for fifteen years mainly inside one man's head now exists in print, where anybody at all can check it. Two more volumes are planned.
suggested_refs: Sophus Lie and Friedrich Engel, Theorie der Transformationsgruppen, vol. I (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1888)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Leipzig, the letter about Killing
stops.date_confidence: attested as a quotation: David E. Rowe's Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography supplement article prints the sentence and dates the letter to early 1888, written on Lie's seeing the first instalment of Killing's four-part study in Mathematische Annalen. No German text or archive location is given by that source, and the letter was not consulted directly. Day unknown.
stops.campa: Wilhelm Killing, working in near-isolation, publishes in Mathematische Annalen the first instalment of a four-part study classifying the structures Lie has spent fifteen years building. Lie reads it as theft, and worse, as theft his own collaborator failed to warn him about. He writes to Klein in the first weeks of the year. Killing had reached the classification of the simple Lie algebras independently, by a different road, and it is still the classification anyone uses.
stops.quote: Mr. Killing's work ... is a gross outrage against me, and I hold Engel responsible.
stops.quote_source: Lie to Felix Klein, early 1888, quoted in David E. Rowe, 'Lie, Marius Sophus,' Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (supplement)
suggested_refs: Wilhelm Killing's four-part study in Mathematische Annalen, 1888-1890, classifying the simple Lie algebras
sources: David E. Rowe, 'Lie, Marius Sophus,' Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (supplement), reproduced at encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Ilten, the asylum near Hanover
stops.date_confidence: the crisis is attested for November 1889 to June 1890 by English Wikipedia, and German Wikipedia independently supports the reading of it as perniziose Anamie combined with difficulties in his scientific surroundings. The clinic at Ilten is reconstruction: no source fetched names it, though German Wikipedia confirms that Ilten, a district of Sehnde southeast of Hanover, hosts the psychiatric Klinikum Wahrendorff founded by Ferdinand Wahrendorff. The day of 16 November is likewise unattested.
stops.campa: In November he stops sleeping. Light hurts him, his nerves give way, and a physician's report records symptoms severe enough to require confinement. He is placed in a private asylum, by the German tradition the one at Ilten, southeast of Hanover. He is there until the following summer, when Anna comes for him and takes him back to Leipzig. Engel covers the lectures the whole time. Modern medical-historical reading puts the collapse down largely to pernicious anaemia, undiagnosed and in that decade untreatable, rather than to madness.
suggested_refs: Klinikum Wahrendorff at Ilten, the private asylum founded by Ferdinand Wahrendorff, named by the German tradition as the place of Lie's confinement
sources: Dossier's citation of Fritzsche in Historia Mathematica (1991) for the Ilten identification

stops.name: Leipzig, the second volume and the man who comes back
stops.date_confidence: Volume II is attested for 1890 (MacTutor); the hospitalisation is attested as running to June 1890 (English Wikipedia). The month here marks the return rather than the publication, neither of which is dated to a day in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Volume II of Theorie der Transformationsgruppen comes out while its principal author is confined in another state. He is back in Leipzig by the summer and back at the board by the winter, and something in him has shifted. He is suspicious now, quick to see plagiarism, quick to count who has taken what from whom. His colleagues put it down to the illness. Later historians point out that a good deal of what he suspected was true, and that a man may be ill and correct at the same time.
suggested_refs: Sophus Lie and Friedrich Engel, Theorie der Transformationsgruppen, vol. II (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1890)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Leipzig, Helmholtz reopened and the Scheffers volumes
stops.date_confidence: the Leipzig chair and years are attested (MacTutor, English Wikipedia); the specific date of resumption after the illness, the Riemann-Helmholtz work and the Scheffers lecture volumes come from the dossier's synthesis and were not independently re-fetched. Month and day are placeholders for ordering.
stops.campa: He resumes full teaching and takes up the Riemann-Helmholtz space problem: what assumptions about the free mobility of rigid bodies force a space to have constant curvature. Hermann von Helmholtz had answered the question in 1868. Lie shows the answer incomplete and redoes it with his own group-theoretic machinery. With Georg Scheffers he brings out a run of lecture-based volumes through the middle nineties, on differential equations, on contact transformations, on continuous groups. He publishes as much as he ever has, and by every account of these years he is harder to work with than he was.
suggested_refs: Lie and Scheffers, the Leipzig lecture volumes of the 1890s; Lie's treatment of the Riemann-Helmholtz space problem
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'
Dossier's synthesis on the Helmholtz critique and the Scheffers volumes

stops.name: Leipzig, the preface to Volume III
stops.date_confidence: attested: MacTutor gives Volume III for 1893 and records that its preface publicly rejected the claim that Lie had been Klein's pupil, damaging his standing among German colleagues. The quotation is from David E. Rowe's DSB supplement article; MacTutor renders the same passage differently, as 'I am no pupil of Klein, nor is the opposite the case, although this might be closer to the truth.' Neither source supplies the original German. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: The third and last volume of Theorie der Transformationsgruppen appears, and in the preface Lie settles his accounts in public. He denies in print, in a technical treatise, that he was ever Klein's pupil. Twenty-four years after Berlin the friendship is over on paper, in front of the whole German mathematical profession, and the profession takes Klein's side. His standing in Germany never recovers. Two translators have put the sentence into English and they do not agree on the wording; no source gives the German.
stops.quote: I am no pupil of Klein's. Nor is the reverse the case, even though it perhaps comes closer to the truth.
stops.quote_source: Preface to Theorie der Transformationsgruppen, vol. III (1893), quoted in David E. Rowe, 'Lie, Marius Sophus,' Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (supplement)
suggested_refs: Sophus Lie and Friedrich Engel, Theorie der Transformationsgruppen, vol. III (Leipzig: B. G. Teubner, 1893), preface
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'
David E. Rowe, 'Lie, Marius Sophus,' Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (supplement), reproduced at encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Leipzig, what Klein wrote where nobody would see it
stops.date_confidence: the quotation is attested verbatim in David E. Rowe's DSB supplement article, which cites Klein's private papers at the Niedersachsische Staats- und Universitatsbibliothek Gottingen, Cod. Ms. F. Klein, 22f. Rowe states neither a date nor a recipient; the date given here is the atlas's own ordering device and carries no evidential weight. The stop sits at Lie's own Leipzig pin, since the note is Klein's writing about Lie's books, not a place Lie went.
stops.campa: Klein answers nothing in public. Among his private papers there is an undated note setting down what he makes of the Lie and Scheffers volumes: that they are the true Lie, the Lie of 1869 to 1872, filled out with careful historical work and Scheffers's drawings, and that they stop dead exactly where his own contribution to the story would have to begin. He gives the reason a name. The sheet stays in Gottingen, in Cod. Ms. F. Klein 22f, and is not printed for most of a century.
stops.quote: That is the true Lie, as he was from 1869-1872, supplemented and completed by careful historical and comparative studies along with excellent drawings by Scheffers. But he breaks off everywhere where my complementary investigations or our collaborative work begins. Why? That's the spirit of latent jealousy.
stops.quote_source: Felix Klein, private papers, Niedersachsische Staats- und Universitatsbibliothek Gottingen, Cod. Ms. F. Klein, 22f, quoted in David E. Rowe, 'Lie, Marius Sophus,' Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (supplement)
suggested_refs: Klein's Nachlass at Gottingen, Cod. Ms. F. Klein 22f, and the asymmetry of the surviving Lie-Klein correspondence
sources: David E. Rowe, 'Lie, Marius Sophus,' Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (supplement), reproduced at encyclopedia.com

stops.name: Leipzig, the honours arrive from everywhere
stops.date_confidence: each election is separately attested: honorary member of the London Mathematical Society 1878 and corresponding member of the Academie des Sciences 1892 (English Wikipedia); Foreign Member of the Royal Society 1895 (MacTutor); Foreign Associate of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences 1895 and the first Lobachevsky Prize 1897 (English Wikipedia). The stop is dated to 1895 to gather them; Lie travelled to none of these places to receive them.
stops.campa: The honours arrive from everywhere and he collects them without leaving Saxony. The London Mathematical Society had made him an honorary member as far back as 1878. The Academie des Sciences in Paris elects him a corresponding member in 1892; the Royal Society of London and the National Academy of Sciences in Washington both take him as a foreign member in 1895; in 1897 Kazan awards him the first Lobachevsky Prize, for the theory of transformation groups. He is fifty-two the year London and Washington elect him.
suggested_refs: The first Lobachevsky Prize, Kazan, 1897; the election registers of the Royal Society and the Academie des Sciences
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Leipzig, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: English Wikipedia gives May 1898 for the resignation and MacTutor corroborates the departure. The exact day of 22 May appears in no source fetched and is reconstruction from the dossier's citation of Fritzsche.
stops.campa: He tenders his resignation of the Leipzig chair in May, giving the climate of the city as bad for his health. Twelve years in Saxony end in an argument he lost and an illness nobody has yet named. Norway has been holding a place for him since 1894, when the Storting voted a second personal professorship to bring him home; the salary is reported at ten thousand kroner and Bjornstjerne Bjornson is said to have campaigned for it in the press, though neither detail appears in any reference article that could be checked.
suggested_refs: The Storting's 1894 act creating a second personal professorship for Lie at Christiania
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Christiania, the chair Norway kept open
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: MacTutor gives September 1898 for the return to Christiania and the taking up of the specially created position. Day unknown.
stops.campa: He comes back to Christiania in September and takes up the chair Norway made for him a second time. He is fifty-five and cannot work a full day. The students who come to the lectures find a large, worn, courteous man who was famous in Germany and is now again the only mathematician of his kind in the country. The position had been voted four years earlier and kept open against his coming, a salary paid to an empty room until he was ready to walk into it. He has been away twelve years. He has about five months.
suggested_refs: The second personal professorship at the Royal Frederick University, occupied from September 1898
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Kristiania, a prize in Abel's name
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia's history of the Abel Prize: Lie began the effort in 1899 on learning that Nobel's planned prizes would exclude mathematics, and Ludvig Sylow and Carl Stormer drew up statutes and rules. Since Lie died on 18 February 1899, the window is the last weeks of his life. Day unknown.
stops.campa: Word reaches Norway that the prizes Alfred Nobel has provided for in his will will not include mathematics. Lie, dying, sets about a Norwegian answer: a prize in the name of Abel, whose collected works he had spent eight years editing with Sylow, to be founded for the centenary of Abel's birth. Sylow and Carl Stormer draw up statutes and rules. Then Lie dies in February, the effort loses its engine, and in 1905 the dissolution of the union with Sweden ends the first attempt altogether. The Abel Prize is announced in 2001 and first actually awarded in 2003.
suggested_refs: The 1899 draft statutes for an Abel prize by Lie, Sylow and Carl Stormer

stops.name: Kristiania, death at fifty-six
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor, English Wikipedia and Store norske leksikon alike: 18 February 1899, Kristiania, pernicious anaemia. The identification of the disease around Christmas 1898 is reconstruction from the dossier's citation of Fritzsche. The figure of roughly 245 publications is likewise reconstruction, found in no reference source consulted. No deathbed address was confirmed; the pin is the historic city centre.
stops.campa: He dies in Kristiania on the eighteenth of February, aged fifty-six. The doctors had put a name to it around Christmas: pernicious anaemia, for which there was no treatment and would be none until the nineteen-twenties, when liver extract and then B12 turned a fatal disease into a managed one. He had been home five months. The publications are said to run to something in the order of two hundred and forty-five, a figure that appears in no reference source consulted and is carried here as an estimate.
suggested_refs: Fritzsche's medical-historical reconstruction of Lie's pernicious anaemia and its diagnosis in December 1898
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Marius Sophus Lie'

stops.name: Var Frelsers gravlund, the western section
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Var Frelsers gravlund is attested by Norwegian Wikipedia, both in Lie's own article and in the cemetery article, which lists him by name in the Vestre del; English Wikipedia's cemetery article carries the entry with a citation-needed tag. The date of 24 February is the date given for Sylow's memorial address; an earlier pass of this research wrongly gave 18 February, which is the date of death. The memorial address itself appears in no source fetched and is reconstruction.
stops.campa: He is buried in the western section of Var Frelsers gravlund, the cemetery in central Oslo where Norway keeps its writers and its statesmen. Ludvig Sylow, who lectured him on Galois thirty-seven years before and edited Abel with him for eight, is recorded as giving the memorial address on the twenty-fourth of February. Anna and their son Herman are laid in the same grave in time. The stone survives in a photograph catalogued at Wikimedia Commons. The grave is not one of the cemetery's formally designated graves of honour.
suggested_refs: Var Frelsers gravlund, Vestre del, Oslo; the Wikimedia Commons photograph of Lie's gravestone

stops.name: Blindern, the auditorium and the collected works
stops.date_confidence: undated: no dedication date for Sophus Lies auditorium was found in any source, and Store norske leksikon states only the present institutional fact. The year here is an ordering device with no evidential weight, chosen to sit at the close of the Gesammelte Abhandlungen, whose seven volumes are attested for 1922-1960 by English Wikipedia. The Werenskiold portrait of 1902 is carried from Store norske leksikon and was not independently re-fetched.
stops.campa: At the university's Blindern campus, built long after his death, a lecture theatre carries his name: Sophus Lies auditorium, under the faculty of mathematics and natural sciences. A monument stands at Nordfjordeid where he was born. Erik Werenskiold painted his portrait in 1902, three years too late to paint him from life. The seven volumes of the Gesammelte Abhandlungen came out between 1922 and 1960, edited chiefly by Friedrich Engel, who had come north to Christiania at twenty-three, and by Poul Heegaard.
suggested_refs: Sophus Lies auditorium, Blindern campus, University of Oslo; the Nordfjordeid monument; Gesammelte Abhandlungen, 7 vols. (Teubner and Aschehoug, 1922-1960)
